1. The substance of the universe is obedient and yielding. The reason that governs it has nothing in itself that would cause it to do evil, because it has no malice: it does evil to nothing, and nothing is harmed by it. Everything comes into being and is brought to completion according to this reason.

2. Let it make no difference to you whether you are cold or warm, as long as you are doing your duty; whether you are drowsy or have had enough sleep; whether people speak badly of you or praise you; whether you are dying or doing something else. For dying, too, is one of the acts of life. So in this act as well, it is enough to do well the task in hand.
3. Look within. Do not let the particular quality of anything, or its worth, escape you.
4. All things that exist will soon change. Either—if indeed all substance is one—they will be turned into vapor, or they will be scattered.
5. The governing reason knows what state it is in, what it does, and what material it works on.
6. The best way to take revenge is not to become like the person who wronged you.
7. Take pleasure in one thing and rest in it: moving from one act done for the common good to another, with God in mind.
8. The ruling faculty is what wakes itself up and directs itself. It makes itself whatever it is and whatever it wants to be, and it also makes everything that happens appear to it the way it wants.

9. Everything is brought about in keeping with the nature of the universe. Certainly nothing is brought about in keeping with some other nature—whether a nature that encloses this nature of the universe from outside, or one contained within it, or one that stands outside it and is independent of it.

10. The universe is either a jumble, a tangle of things that are thrown together and scattered again, or it is unity, order and providence. If it is the first, why do I want to linger in a random mixture of things, in such a mess? Why should I care about anything except how I shall one day become earth? And why am I troubled, when my elements will be scattered whatever I do? But if the second is true, then I feel reverence, I stand firm, and I trust in the one who governs.

11. When circumstances have forced you off balance in some way, come back to yourself quickly, and do not stay out of tune any longer than you are forced to be. For you will master the harmony better by returning to it again and again.

12. If you had a stepmother and a mother at the same time, you would do your duty by your stepmother, but you would still keep going back to your mother. Let the court and philosophy be your stepmother and your mother now. Go back often to philosophy and rest in her. It is through her that what you meet at court seems bearable to you, and that you seem bearable to the court.

13. When we have meat and other such food in front of us, we take in the impression that this is the dead body of a fish, and this the dead body of a bird or a pig. And again, that this Falernian wine is only a little grape juice, and this purple robe some sheep's wool dyed with the blood of a shellfish. These impressions reach the things themselves and go right through them, and so we see what kind of things they really are. We ought to do the same all through life. Where things seem most worthy of our approval, we should strip them bare, look at how worthless they are, and take away all the words that make them sound grand. For outward show is a powerful twister of reason; and just when you are most sure that you are busy with things worth your trouble, that is when it deceives you most. Consider, then, what Crates says about Xenocrates himself.

14. Most of the things the crowd admires belong to the most basic kind: things held together simply by cohesion or by natural growth, such as stones, wood, fig trees, vines and olives. People who are a little more reasonable admire things held together by a principle of life, such as flocks and herds. People who are more educated still admire things held together by a rational soul. But they do not mean the soul that is rational in the universal sense. They value a soul only for being skilled in some craft or clever in some other way, or simply for owning a large number of slaves. But someone who values the rational soul—the soul that is universal and made for life as a citizen—cares about nothing else. Above all, he keeps his own soul in a condition and an activity that fit reason and life in community, and he works toward this together with those who are of the same kind as himself.

15. Some things are rushing into existence, and others are rushing out of it; and of what is coming into existence, part has already gone out. Motion and change are always renewing the world, just as the unbroken passage of time is always renewing the endless length of the ages. In this river, then, where nothing stands still, which of the things rushing past would anyone value highly? It would be like falling in love with one of the sparrows flying by—and it has already gone out of sight. The very life of each person is something like this: like the vapor given off by the blood, and the drawing in of air. For we breathe in the air once and give it back, as we do every moment; and giving back the whole power of breathing is just the same. You received that power at your birth, yesterday or the day before, and you give it back to the element from which you first drew it.

16. What is worth valuing is not giving off moisture, as plants do; nor breathing, as tame animals and wild beasts do; nor receiving impressions from the appearances of things; nor being jerked about by desires like a puppet on strings; nor gathering in herds; nor taking in food—for that is no better than separating out and getting rid of the useless part of our food. What, then, is worth valuing? Being received with clapping hands? No. Nor should we value the clapping of tongues; for the praise of the many is only a clapping of tongues. Suppose, then, that you have given up this worthless thing called fame: what is left that is worth valuing? This, I think: to move yourself and to hold yourself back in keeping with your own proper makeup. That is the end to which all occupations and crafts lead. For every craft aims at this: that what has been made should be fitted to the work it was made for. The vine-grower who tends the vine, the horse-breaker, and the dog-trainer all seek this end. The upbringing and teaching of the young aim at something too. Here, then, is where the value of upbringing and teaching lies. If you have this right, you will not look for anything else. Will you not stop valuing many other things as well? If not, you will be neither free, nor sufficient for your own happiness, nor free from passion. For you are bound to be envious, jealous and suspicious of those who can take those things away, and to plot against those who have what you value. Anyone who needs any of those things is bound to be in complete turmoil; and besides, he is bound to find fault with the gods again and again. But to respect and honor your own mind will make you content with yourself, in harmony with society, and in agreement with the gods—that is, praising everything they give and have ordered.

17. Above, below, all around, the elements are in motion. But the motion of virtue is not among these. It is something more divine: moving forward along a path hard to see, it goes happily on its way.

18. How strangely people behave! They will not praise those who live at the same time as they do and live alongside them; yet being praised themselves by later generations, by people they have never seen and never will see—this they value highly. But that is much the same as being upset because the people who lived before you did not praise you.

19. If something is hard for you to do, do not suppose it is impossible for a human being. But if something is possible for a human being and in keeping with human nature, believe that you can achieve it too.

20. In athletic training, suppose someone has clawed you with his nails and given you a wound by crashing into your head. Well, we do not show any sign of annoyance, we do not take offense, and we do not suspect him afterward of being treacherous. We are on our guard against him, yes—but not as an enemy, and not with suspicion; we simply keep out of his way without fuss. Let your behavior be something like this in all the other parts of life. Let us overlook a great deal in those who are like our opponents in the gymnasium. For, as I said, it is in our power to keep out of the way, and to feel neither suspicion nor hatred.

21. If anyone can convince me and show me that I am wrong in what I think or do, I will gladly change. For I am looking for the truth, and no one has ever been harmed by the truth. The one who is harmed is the person who stays in his error and ignorance.
22. I do my duty; other things do not trouble me. For those other things are either lifeless, or without reason, or things that have wandered off and do not know the way.

23. As for animals that have no reason, and things and objects in general: you have reason and they have none, so make use of them in a generous and open-handed spirit. But treat human beings, since they have reason, in a spirit of fellowship. And on every occasion call on the gods. Do not worry about how long you will go on doing this; even three hours spent this way are enough.

24. Alexander of Macedon and his stable hand were brought to the same state by death. Either they were taken back into the same generative principles of the universe, or they were both scattered alike among the atoms.

25. Consider how many things happen in each of us in the same indivisible moment—things of the body and things of the soul. Then you will not be surprised that many more things, or rather all the things that come into being, exist at the same time in the one whole that is everything, which we call the Cosmos.

26. If someone asked you how the name Antoninus is spelled, would you strain your voice and shout out each letter? And if they got angry, would you get angry too? Would you not calmly go on and name each letter in turn? In the same way, remember that in this life too every duty is made up of certain parts. Your duty is to keep to these, without being flustered and without showing anger toward those who are angry with you, and to go on your way and finish the task set before you.

27. How cruel it is not to let people strive for what seems to them suited to their nature and good for them! Yet in a way you do not let them do this when you resent their doing wrong. For they are certainly drawn toward these things because they suppose them to be suited to their nature and good for them. But what they suppose is not really so. Teach them, then, and show them, without being angry.

28. Death is an end: an end of the impressions that come through the senses, of the tugging of the strings that work our appetites, of the thoughts that run this way and that, and of service to the flesh.
29. It is shameful for the soul to give way first in this life, while your body is not giving way.

30. Take care that you are not turned into a Caesar, that you are not dyed in that dye; for it does happen. So keep yourself simple, good, pure, serious, unpretentious, a friend of justice, a worshipper of the gods, kind, affectionate, and energetic in every fitting act. Strive to remain the person philosophy wanted to make you. Revere the gods, and help people. Life is short. This earthly life has only one fruit: a reverent disposition and acts done for the common good. Do everything as a pupil of Antoninus. Remember how steady he was in every act that reason called for; how even-tempered in everything; his piety; the calm of his face; his gentleness; his disregard for empty fame; and his effort to understand things. Remember how he would never let anything pass until he had examined it very carefully and understood it clearly; how he put up with those who blamed him unjustly without blaming them in return; how he did nothing in a hurry; how he would not listen to slander; how carefully he examined people's characters and actions. He was not given to criticizing people, and he was not timid, or suspicious, or a sophist. Remember how little he was satisfied with, in lodging, bed, clothing, food and servants; how hard-working and patient he was; how, because he ate so sparingly, he could hold out until evening, not even needing to relieve himself except at the usual hour. Remember his firmness and consistency in his friendships; how he put up with people who spoke freely against his opinions; how glad he was when anyone showed him something better; and how religious he was without superstition. Imitate all this, so that when your last hour comes your conscience may be as clear as his.

31. Come back to your senses and call yourself back. Once you have woken from sleep and seen that it was only dreams that troubled you, then, now that you are awake, look at the things around you as you looked at those dreams.

32. I am made of a little body and a soul. To this little body all things are indifferent, because it cannot perceive differences. But to the understanding, only those things are indifferent that are not its own activities. Whatever things are its own activities are all in its power. And even of these, only the ones that concern the present count; for the mind's future and past activities are, for the present, indifferent too.

33. The work the hand does is not against nature, and neither is the work of the foot, as long as the foot does a foot's work and the hand a hand's. In the same way, a human being's labor is not against nature for him as a human being, as long as that labor does a human being's work. And if his labor is not against his nature, it is not bad for him either.
34. How many pleasures have been enjoyed by robbers, by men who murdered their fathers, by tyrants!

35. Do you not see how craftsmen go along up to a point with people who are not skilled in their craft, but still hold on to the principles of their art and will not bear to depart from them? Is it not strange if the architect and the doctor respect the principles of their own crafts more than a human being respects his own reason, which he shares with the gods?

36. Asia and Europe are corners of the universe; the whole sea is a drop in the universe; Mount Athos is a little clod of the universe; all of present time is a point in eternity. All things are small, changeable, perishable. All things come from there—from that ruling power of the universe—either coming directly from it or following from it as consequences. So the lion's gaping jaws, and poison, and every harmful thing, such as a thorn or mud, are by-products of what is grand and beautiful. Do not imagine, then, that they are of a different kind from what you revere; form a true judgment of the source of all things.
37. Whoever has seen the present has seen everything: all that has happened from all eternity, and all that will happen through endless time. For all things are of one kind and one form.

38. Think often about how all things in the universe are connected and related to one another. For in a way all things are woven together, and in this way they are all friendly to one another. One thing follows another in order, and this comes about through the active movement of things, the way they all breathe together as one, and the unity of their substance.
39. Fit yourself to the things that have been allotted to you; and love the people among whom you have been given your place—but love them truly, sincerely.

40. With every instrument, tool or vessel, the one who made it is not there; yet it is doing well if it does what it was made for. But in the things that nature holds together, the power that made them is inside them and stays there. So it is all the more right to revere this power, and to think that if you live and act according to its will, everything in you is in keeping with intelligence. And in the same way, in the universe too, the things that belong to it are in keeping with intelligence.

41. If you suppose that any of the things outside your power are good or bad for you, then it is inevitable that when such a bad thing happens to you, or you lose such a good thing, you will blame the gods and hate people too: those who caused the misfortune or the loss, or those you suspect of being likely to cause it. Indeed, we do much injustice because we treat these things as though they made a difference, instead of seeing them as neither good nor bad. But if we judge only what is in our power to be good or bad, there is no reason left either to find fault with God or to take a hostile stand against any human being.

42. We are all working together toward one end, some knowingly and with understanding, others without knowing what they are doing. So too are people who are asleep: it is Heraclitus, I think, who says that even they are workers and fellow workers in what happens in the universe. But people work together in different ways. Even those who find fault with what happens, and those who try to oppose it and stop it, contribute in full measure; for the universe had need even of people like these. So it remains for you to understand what kind of workers you are placing yourself among. For the one who governs all things will certainly make good use of you, and will take you in as one part among the fellow workers, those whose labors lead to one end. But do not be that kind of part—like the cheap and ridiculous line in the play that Chrysippus speaks of.

43. Does the sun take it on himself to do the work of the rain, or Aesculapius, the god of healing, the work of the Fruit-bearer, the earth? And what about each of the stars—are they not different, and yet do they not work together toward the same end?

44. If the gods have made decisions about me and about what must happen to me, they have decided well; for it is not easy even to imagine a god without forethought. And as for doing me harm, why would they have any wish to do that? What would they gain from it, or what would the whole gain—the whole that is the special object of their providence? But if they have not made decisions about me individually, they have certainly made decisions about the whole, at least; and whatever follows as a consequence of that general arrangement I ought to welcome gladly and be content with. But suppose they make decisions about nothing. It is impious to believe that; or if we do believe it, let us stop sacrificing, praying and swearing by them, and doing everything else we do as though the gods were present and living among us. But if, all the same, the gods make decisions about none of the things that concern us, then I am able to decide about myself, and I can ask what is useful. And what is useful to each person is what is in keeping with his own makeup and nature. My nature is rational and made for community. My city and country, as far as I am Antoninus, is Rome; as far as I am a human being, it is the world. So only the things that are useful to these two cities are useful to me.

45. Whatever happens to each person serves the interest of the whole. That might be enough. But if you look closely, you will also see this as a general truth: whatever is profitable to one person is profitable to other people too. But take the word "profitable" here in its everyday sense, as it is used of things in the middle—things that are neither good nor bad.

46. In the amphitheater and places like it, the constant sight of the same things, and the sameness of it all, make the show tiresome to you. It is the same with the whole of life; for everything, above and below, is the same and comes from the same things. How long, then?

47. Keep thinking of how people of every kind, of every occupation and of every nation, are dead, so that your thoughts come down even to Philistion and Phoebus and Origanion. Now turn your thoughts to the other kinds of people. To that place, then, we must go, where there are so many great orators and so many noble philosophers—Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Socrates; so many heroes of former days, and so many generals after them, and tyrants. Besides these, there are Eudoxus, Hipparchus, Archimedes, and other people of sharp natural talent: great minds, lovers of hard work, versatile, confident, people who even mocked the perishable, short-lived life of human beings, like Menippus and others like him. Think of all these: they have long been in the dust. What harm, then, is that to them? And what harm to those whose names are not known at all? One thing here is worth a great deal: to spend your life in truth and justice, with kindness even toward liars and unjust people.

48. When you want to cheer yourself, think of the good qualities of the people who live with you: the energy of one, the modesty of another, the generosity of a third, some other good quality of a fourth. For nothing gives so much delight as the examples of the virtues when they show themselves in the characters of those who live with us, and appear there in as great abundance as possible. So we must keep them before our eyes.

49. You are not unhappy, I suppose, because you weigh only so many pounds and not three hundred. So do not be unhappy that you must live only so many years and not more. Just as you are satisfied with the amount of stuff you have been given to be made of, be content with your time too.

50. Let us try to persuade people. But act even against their will, when the principles of justice lead that way. If, however, someone uses force to block your way, turn to contentment and calm, and at the same time use the obstacle to practice some other virtue. And remember that you made your attempt with a reservation, that is, conditionally: you did not want to do what was impossible. What, then, did you want?—To make an attempt of just this kind.—And you achieve your aim, even if the things you set out to do are not accomplished.

51. The person who loves fame thinks his own good lies in what other people do; the person who loves pleasure thinks it lies in his own sensations; but the person who has understanding thinks his own good lies in his own actions.
52. It is in our power to hold no opinion about a thing, and not to be troubled in our soul. For things themselves have no natural power to form our judgments.
53. Train yourself to listen carefully to what someone else is saying, and as far as possible, get inside the speaker's mind.
54. What is not good for the swarm is not good for the bee either.

55. If sailors insulted the helmsman, or sick people their doctor, whom else would they listen to? Or how could the helmsman keep the people on board safe, or the doctor bring health to the people he looks after?
56. How many of those who came into the world with me have already left it.

57. To people with jaundice, honey tastes bitter; to people bitten by mad dogs, water is terrifying; and to little children, a ball is a fine thing. Why, then, am I angry? Do you think a false opinion has less power than the bile in someone with jaundice, or the poison in someone bitten by a mad dog?
58. No one will stop you from living according to the reason of your own nature; nothing will happen to you against the reason of the nature of the universe.
59. What kind of people are those whom others want to please, for what ends, and by what kinds of acts? How soon time will cover everything, and how much it has covered already.
